articles.title: 'It’s not 19th century': Kerala CM Satheesan slams cleric over 'women should stay home' remark
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Kerala chief minister VD Satheesan on Wednesday rejected Sunni cleric and Grand Mufti of India Kanthapuram AP Aboobacker Musliyar’s call fo.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Kerala chief minister VD Satheesan on Wednesday rejected Sunni cleric and Grand Mufti of India Kanthapuram AP Aboobacker Musliyar’s call for restrictions on women’s participation in public life. He said women must join the mainstream, asserting that such views have no place in a developing Kerala.Speaking to reporters, Satheesan said the state government did not agree with Aboobacker’s position that women should remain at home, adding that even Islam did not require women to be confined to domestic life."We don't agree with his statement that women should stay home. It's not a suitable stand in our developing Keralam. It's not the 19th century that one should make such statements. Even Islam doesn't say that. Women should not stay home, but join the mainstream. That is our stand," he said.Satheesan’s remarks came amid mounting criticism of Aboobacker over his comments defending restrictions issued by the Kanthapuram faction of the Samastha Kerala Jamiyyathul Ulama on women’s participation in religious events.Labour minister Bindu Krishna also criticised the cleric, saying such remarks undermined women’s constitutional rights and sought to push them "centuries back"."Constitution of India assures equal rights to women and men, irrespective of sex. The people have the right to live a free and liberal life. And also, these types of statements push women centuries back. So, we can't accept such statements. Our women are free to move. They are best rulers. Our girls are always coming through this society, and we can't accept such statements," Krishna told ANI.The controversy followed remarks made by Aboobacker at the Hubbul Rasul Conference in Kochi, where he defended recent directives issued by the Kanthapuram faction of Samastha to local Mahalls on women’s participation in religious celebrations.A circular issued by the organisation directed Madrasas not to allow women to be present among unrelated men at religious events. It also advised against displaying young women on public stages and having them participate in road processions alongside unrelated men.Defending the directives, Aboobacker said women should remain within the home and invoked the Quran to support his position."Women should remain confined within their homes. They should not enter the public sphere. The Holy Quran says so," Aboobacker said, while defending the purdah system as a practice intended to protect women’s dignity.He argued that allowing women into public spaces without restrictions could result in "great destruction", insisting that the measures were intended to honour and protect women rather than diminish them.Aboobacker also said Islam had granted women property and inheritance rights centuries ago to improve their status without requiring them to leave domestic life. He maintained that he was not concerned by opposition or political criticism and said no one could silence him or force him to change Islamic doctrines.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: An Iowa priest vowed to build a shrine if he survived pneumonia; after recovering, he spent 42 years using over 100 train carloads of stone to create it
articles.summary: US News: In the late 19th century, a young seminarian battling a life-threatening bout of pneumonia made a promise that would eventually transform a small Iowa.
articles.body: In the late 19th century, a young seminarian battling a life-threatening bout of pneumonia made a promise that would eventually transform a small Iowa town into the home of one of the world's largest man-made grottos. If he survived, Father Paul Matthias Dobberstein vowed to build a shrine in honour of the Virgin Mary. He recovered and more than a century later, the promise he made has become a vast monument of stone, minerals, fossils and religious art in West Bend, Iowa.Known as the 'Grotto of the Redemption', the extraordinary structure was built over 42 years and incorporates material transported in more than 100 train carloads. The National Register of Historic Places describes it as one of the world's largest man-made grottos and one of the most extensive mosaics ever created.A promise made during illnessDobberstein was born in Rosenfeld, Germany, in 1872 and emigrated to the United States when he was 20. He entered the Seminary of St Francis near Milwaukee, Wisconsin, to prepare for the priesthood. It was during his time at the seminary that he became critically ill with pneumonia. Facing the possibility of death, he prayed to the Virgin Mary and promised that if he recovered, he would build a shrine in her honour.The illness passed, and Dobberstein completed his studies. He was ordained a priest in 1897 and the following year was appointed pastor of Saints Peter and Paul Catholic Church in West Bend, Iowa. West Bend, surrounded by the flat farmland of Iowa, might seem an unlikely location for a monument made from precious and semi-precious stones gathered from around the world. But it was here that Dobberstein began preparing to fulfil his promise.For roughly a decade after arriving in West Bend, he stockpiled rocks, minerals and other geological materials. The actual construction of the grotto began in 1912.Building a shrine without blueprintsDobberstein's project was unlike a conventional building. The Grotto of the Redemption was constructed without formal plans, blueprints or sketches. Instead, the priest developed his vision as he worked, assembling stones into an elaborate series of religious scenes.The project eventually grew into nine interconnected grottos depicting the Christian story of redemption, beginning with the Garden of Eden and continuing through the birth and life of Jesus, the Crucifixion and finally the Resurrection.The site contains 26 religious stations and 65 statues carved from Carrara marble by Italian sculptors. Beneath and around the statues are hundreds of thousands of stones and geological specimens, creating a mosaic-like landscape unlike anything else in the region.The materials came from remarkably diverse places. The National Register documentation records stones from every US state as well as locations around the world. Among them are alexandrite associated with Russian emerald mines, amethyst from the Andes, jade from China, lapis lazuli from the Near East and a rock brought back from Admiral Richard Byrd's expedition to the South Pole. One grotto alone contains 65 tons of petrified wood.More than 100 train carloads of materialThe scale of Dobberstein's undertaking is perhaps best understood through the amount of material required. More than 100 train carloads of rocks and stones were eventually used to create the grotto. These stones had to be collected, transported, sorted, processed and carefully positioned. The National Register records that Dobberstein travelled widely in search of geological treasures and faced bad roads, difficult weather and inadequate transportation. He also suffered injuries in automobile and construction accidents, but repeatedly returned to his work. For decades, much of the construction was carried out almost entirely by hand.Until 1947, cement, mortar, rocks, steel and precious stones were moved around the site using buckets and wheelbarrows. By then, roughly 80% of the project had been completed. An electric hoist was finally installed to help the ageing priest continue his work.Dobberstein was assisted by Matthew Szerensce, whom he reportedly regarded as his "good right hand". The two worked alongside each other from the early stages of construction.A 42-year labour of faithWhat began as a promise made by a sick seminarian eventually consumed much of Dobberstein's adult life. He continued working on the Grotto of the Redemption while serving as a priest in West Bend. By the time he died in July 1954, he had spent 42 years turning his vision into reality. His physical condition had deteriorated in his later years, and Szerensce and Father Louis Greving eventually carried forward his plans. Construction and additions continued after Dobberstein's death.The National Register notes that the Grotto represents an exceptionally large collection of semi-precious stones, ores, minerals, fossils, petrified material, coral and shells concentrated in one location. It also helped inspire a broader tradition of decorative grotto construction across the Upper Midwest.From personal promise to historic landmarkThe Grotto of the Redemption was eventually recognised for its architectural and artistic significance. It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places, with the nomination describing it as a particularly significant example of regional grotto construction and one of the world's largest man-made grottos.Today, visitors entering the site encounter a maze of stone-covered structures, arches, chapels and sculptures. The geological material is not merely decorative. It forms an integral part of Dobberstein's attempt to tell a religious story through the natural beauty of stone. A promise made during a desperate illness had therefore evolved into a monumental lifetime project.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: In 1991, Harvard Forest buried heating cables 10 cm deep to warm Massachusetts soil by 5°C; after 26 years, warmed plots had lost 17% of carbon stored in the top 60 cm  2. redundancy
articles.summary: US News: A long-term experiment at Harvard Forest shows that warming temperatures can significantly affect the carbon cycle in forest soils, leading to a complex interaction between microbial activity and organic matter decomposition.
articles.body: Beneath a Massachusetts forest, scientists had been deliberately warming the soil for more than two decades to study how rising temperatures affected the carbon stored underground. According to Harvard Forest, the experiment began in 1991 at the Prospect Hill Tract in Petersham, Massachusetts, within an even-aged mixed hardwood forest. Researchers established heated plots alongside control plots and used resistance cables buried about 10 cm below the soil surface to keep the warmed plots roughly 5°C above ambient soil temperatures. By the time of a major study published in 2017, the experiment had provided 26 years of observations on soil respiration, carbon dioxide emissions, soil moisture, nitrogen cycling and other processes, allowing researchers to examine how sustained warming altered the forest’s underground carbon and nitrogen cycles.Heating the soil beneath the forestAt the Prospect Hill site, resistance cables were buried about 10 centimetres below the soil surface. The heated plots were maintained at temperatures roughly 5°C above those of the control plots, with sensors and automated equipment regulating the temperature difference. The experiment was designed to examine how warming affects fundamental soil processes, particularly the cycling of carbon and nitrogen. Forest soils contain organic matter made up partly of material derived from fallen leaves, roots and other biological remains. Microorganisms break down this material, releasing carbon dioxide as they respire. Warming can accelerate microbial activity, potentially increasing the rate at which carbon moves from soil into the atmosphere.But the Harvard Forest experiment showed that the soil-carbon response did not remain constant throughout the study. During the first decade, the warmed plots released more carbon dioxide than the control plots, and researchers estimated that they had lost about 11% of the carbon stored in the upper 60 centimetres of soil. The difference in carbon dioxide emissions between the warmed and control plots then diminished for several years, including a period when the plots showed little separation. This changing response suggested that microbial activity depended not only on temperature but also on the amount and composition of organic matter available in the soil. As the experiment continued, the researchers observed further changes in the soil-carbon response, showing that the effects of long-term warming could not be described as a simple, constant rate of carbon loss.A 26-year experiment revealed a changing responseAccording to research published in Science, the Harvard Forest warming experiment had recorded 26 years of observations by 2017, and the warmed plots held about 17% less carbon in organic matter in the upper 60 centimetres of soil than the control plots. The researchers found that carbon loss did not occur at a constant rate. Warming initially increased soil carbon emissions, but the difference between heated and control plots became undetectable between 2001 and 2007 before carbon release increased again from 2008 to 2013 and later declined towards control levels. The researchers linked these changes partly to shifts in the soil microbial community, including a greater role for organisms capable of decomposing more resistant organic matter such as lignin. As easily decomposed material became depleted, the microbial community changed, and the rate of carbon release also changed.What the experiment means for a warming worldThe experiment was designed to isolate the effects of sustained soil warming by raising temperatures by about 5°C, allowing researchers to examine how changes in temperature influenced soil carbon processes under controlled conditions. This level of warming was larger and more abrupt than the gradual warming experienced at many natural forest sites, so the experiment was not intended to reproduce a specific future climate scenario. Instead, it provided a way to investigate the mechanisms through which warming can alter carbon stored in forest soils. Forests are not only places where trees remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere; their soils also contain large quantities of organic carbon, and temperature changes can affect how quickly that material is decomposed and released.Harvard Forest still focuses on the impact of climate warming on soil organic matter and microbes. According to a recent study using the same long-term warming experiment, decades of warming affected soil organic matter, providing further evidence that warming can influence below-ground carbon processes over long periods. The broader lesson from Harvard Forest is about the invisible processes beneath the forest floor, not just a single percentage. Microbes change their behaviour, organic matter is transformed, and the carbon input and output in the soil varies with time. As a result of decades of heating several specific plots, researchers had a unique opportunity to observe this process. This experiment offers an unusual glimpse into the future of one of the planet’s least understood carbon sinks under climate warming.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Four people in court charged over Wincobank newborn baby death
articles.summary: Four people, aged between 19 and 38, appear in court charged with murdering the newborn.
articles.body:
Two men and two women have appeared in court charged with murdering a baby girl found stabbed to death at a house in Sheffield.

The newborn - referred to as Baby S in court - was found at a property in Holywell Heights, in the Wincobank area, on Sunday, after police were called to reports of concern for her safety.

Slovakian nationals Andrea Skopova, 20, formerly of Robey Street, Sheffield appeared at Sheffield Magistrates' Court alongside Peter Horvath, 19, Nina Horvathova, 37 and Peter Horvath, 38, all of of Holywell Heights.

They have been charged with murder, causing or allowing the death of a child and perverting the course of justice by taking steps to conceal the killing of an infant.

A fifth person, a 15-year-old girl, who cannot be named for legal reasons, has charged with perverting the course of justice.

After a brief hearing the four adult defendants were remanded into custody to appear at Sheffield Crown Court on Thursday.

Earlier police said that two women, 26 and 37, who were arrested on suspicion of murder remained on bail.

Speaking ahead of the court hearing, Det Ch Insp Tom Woodward said: "This is a significant step in our investigation into the tragic circumstances that resulted in the death of this baby girl.

"I would like to thank our communities, who I know will have been deeply impacted by this traumatic incident, for supporting us as we work through this intricate investigation.

"We would ask the public to avoid speculating and posting information online about this case while the legal process takes it course.

"Protecting the integrity of the criminal justice process is crucial to us securing justice for this little girl."

Police said officers would continue to be in and around the Holywell Heights area carrying out inquiries.

articles.title: From Sushant Singh Rajput 'link' to CBI probe: The Disha Salian case so far
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: The Bombay High Court on Wednesday ordered the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) to register an FIR and take over the investigation int.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Bombay High Court on Wednesday ordered the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) to register an FIR and take over the investigation into the death of Disha Salian, former manager of actor Sushant Singh Rajput, who died in June 2020.A bench of Justices Sarang Kotwal and Ranjitsinha Raja Bhonsale directed Mumbai Police to hand over all case records to the CBI and ordered that the probe be conducted by a suitably experienced and senior officer.The court also pulled up Mumbai Police over the manner and duration of its investigation, saying it had continued for about six years without an FIR being registered. The bench observed that the police investigation “raises more questions than it answers” and said a CBI probe was necessary.The 44-page judgment said there were “glaring discrepancies” in the police investigation and called for a “proper and substantive” probe.“In this case, we are of the opinion that the police had sufficient opportunity to investigate the offence, but they have not registered the FIR and have not carried out the investigation of a cognisable offence,” the court said.Reacting to the order, Salian’s father Satish Salian, who has pursued the case for six years and alleged that his daughter was murdered, said he felt “relieved” but had no reason to celebrate after losing his daughter.“I have been waiting for this for 6 years. There is no reason to be happy. I have lost my daughter. I feel relieved today. That's all,” he told reporters, adding that he had folded his hands and thanked the judge.What is the case?Disha Salian was found dead on June 8, 2020, after falling from the 14th floor of a residential building in Mumbai’s Malad area. Mumbai Police registered an Accidental Death Report (ADR) and, after an inquiry, maintained that she had died by suicide.Salian’s father challenged the police’s handling of the case and approached the Bombay High Court, alleging that his daughter had been gang-raped and murdered.He also alleged a politically orchestrated cover-up to protect influential people and sought registration of an FIR and a CBI investigation, including into allegations against Shiv Sena (UBT) MLA Aaditya Thackeray.The high court, however, made it clear that it was not expressing any opinion on the allegations against any individual. It said the CBI would have to determine whether the evidence gathered during its investigation warranted treating anyone as an accused.The court pointed to several aspects of the investigation that it said required closer examination. One issue was the spot panchnama, or the record of the scene where Salian’s body was found, which the court noted had been conducted belatedly.The bench also questioned the absence of blood at the spot. It raised doubts about whether the injuries recorded in the case were consistent with a fall from such a height.“If the deceased had fallen on her face from the 12th floor, then it is difficult to accept that there was only one injury on the chin of the body. Not a single facial bone was fractured. We find this difficult to accept,” the court said, as quoted by PTI.During an earlier hearing, the court had also questioned how a fall from such height could result in such limited injuries. The prosecution had argued that Salian suffered severe facial, skull and rib fractures and that rain could have washed away blood from the spot. The court noted that the rain cited by the prosecution had occurred several hours after the incident.The bench also noted an apparent discrepancy concerning Salian’s clothing. It observed that while the panchnama and post-mortem report stated that her body had no clothes, photographs from the hospital and morgue appeared to show her wearing clothes.“There is room for reasonable doubt in all these aspects. However, we are not drawing any conclusion at this stage,” the court said.The court had also earlier questioned why Mumbai Police had registered only an ADR despite the allegations raised by Salian’s family. It noted that copies of the post-mortem report and ADR had not been provided to the family even years after her death.Salian’s lawyer Nilesh Ojha had alleged discrepancies in the post-mortem report and argued that an FIR should have been registered on the basis of the allegations and material placed before the authorities.What has the HC ordered?The High Court directed the CBI to record Satish Salian’s statement and register an FIR. Mumbai Police was ordered to hand over all papers and records relating to the case to the central agency “forthwith”.The CBI has been asked to appoint a suitably experienced and senior officer to investigate the case.The court also imposed an important safeguard: no individual can be treated as an accused merely on the basis of the allegations made before the court.“Nobody shall be treated as an accused unless in the opinion of the investigating officer there are sufficient grounds to raise reasonable suspicion against him depending on the material collected during the investigation,” the court said.The bench also said that if the investigation finds that no criminal case is made out, the CBI must file an appropriate summary report before the competent court.“In case the investigation reveals that no case is made out, then the CBI shall file the appropriate summary report before the court concerned,” it said.Satish Salian will be free to challenge such a report and file objections before the court.The high court described Salian as an “unfortunate” father who had lost his young daughter in “tragic circumstances” and said the matter required a substantive investigation. At the same time, it refrained from commenting on the allegations made against specific individuals.Satish Salian’s petition sought an FIR and investigation into allegations against Shiv Sena (UBT) leader Aaditya Thackeray, son of former Maharashtra chief minister Uddhav Thackeray.The court however did not make any adverse finding against Thackeray and said it was for the investigating agency to examine the evidence.Thackeray had separately approached the high court seeking to intervene in the proceedings. In his application, he described Satish Salian’s petition as “false, frivolous and motivated” and sought an opportunity to be heard before any order was passed.Sushant Singh Rajput 'link'The case has also drawn attention because Salian had briefly worked as a manager for actor Sushant Singh Rajput.Rajput was found dead at his Bandra residence on June 14, 2020, six days after Salian’s death. The proximity of the two deaths led to widespread speculation, although the cases were investigated separately.A CBI probe was also ordered into Rajput’s death. The agency subsequently filed a closure report stating that he died by suicide; the concerned court is yet to decide on the report.The latest order does not establish that Salian was murdered or that the allegations made by her family are true. It instead directs a fresh investigation by the CBI after finding that the police probe contained issues that, in the court’s view, warranted further examination.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Meet Yanin ‘Proud’, a 17-year-old Thai student who built artificial hornbill nests from recycled plastic and won two global conservation awards
articles.summary: Rest of World News: At just 17, Thai student Yanin ‘Proud’ Tangkaravakoon has turned a concern for endangered hornbills into a unique conservation project that gives disc.
articles.body: At just 17, Thai student Yanin ‘Proud’ Tangkaravakoon has turned a concern for endangered hornbills into a unique conservation project that gives discarded waste plastic a new purpose. Her initiative, ‘Homes for Hornbills’ creates artificial nests designed to provide breeding spaces for hornbills as natural tree cavities become harder to find. The project has now earned her two major international honours, including recognition from ‘The Earth Prize’ and National Geographic’s ‘Slingshot Challenge.’ According to Khaosod English, the project combines wildlife conservation, recycled materials and community involvement to address the declining populations of hornbills in Thailand. The Nation reported that the nests have been developed with attention to the birds’ behaviour, safety and the environmental conditions they face. What began with a young student’s fascination with these distinctive birds has grown into a practical conservation effort with encouraging early results.How did this 17-year-old Thai student turn recycled plastic into artificial hornbill nestsAccording to Khaosod English, Yanin’s interest in hornbills began during a primary school field trip to Khao Yai National Park. Fascinated by the birds, she later learned more about the threats affecting their survival and began working towards a solution. The result was ‘Homes for Hornbills,’ a project built around the idea of creating durable artificial nesting spaces from upcycled materials, including discarded plastic bottles. The initiative was developed in collaboration with the ‘Thailand Hornbill Research Foundation’ and goes beyond simply placing artificial nests in forests.The wider conservation model has three main parts. Providing nests designed around hornbill behaviour, teaching students about conservation and developing long-term ways to work with communities in order to reduce pressures such as poaching and deforestation. The idea addresses a particularly important problem for hornbills. The Nation explained that, unlike many birds, hornbills cannot simply build their own nests. They depend on naturally formed cavities in large trees for breeding. As forests disappear and human activity alters their habitats, these suitable nesting sites are becoming increasingly difficult to find.The nest design was developed to solve the weaknesses of older optionsArtificial nests are not entirely new, but Yanin’s project sought to improve on some of the problems associated with existing designs. As per The Nation, traditional wooden nests can deteriorate within 2-3 years and require additional timber. Earthen jar nests may provide limited internal space, potentially restricting the movement and development of young birds. Fibreglass composite nests can last longer, but their glass fibres may also raise concerns about possible irritation over time. Homes for Hornbills therefore explored a different approach. ‘Discarded plastic bottles’ were transformed into resin-based materials, while natural fibres were used instead of conventional glass fibres.Yanin worked with researchers from the Thailand Hornbill Research Foundation to refine important features of the nests, including their size, ventilation, durability and safety for the birds. The project also received support from TOA Venture Holding’s polymer laboratory, where different natural fibres were tested. According to The Nation, hemp showed particularly strong performance during testing because of its ability to absorb the material effectively and resist bending. After adjustments to the fibre mixture and the plastic-based material, the resulting nests were designed to be durable enough to remain functional for up to 10 years.The artificial nests are already giving hornbills new breeding opportunitiesThe project has moved beyond the testing stage and into the field. The Nation reported that ‘20 artificial nests’ have been installed on Yao Noi Island in southern Thailand. The early results have been encouraging. During the 2025 breeding season, 10 nests were occupied and 14 hornbill chicks successfully fledged. Khaosod English described the project as involving local students and community members, showing that the initiative is intended to create wider participation rather than operate solely as a scientific experiment. 60 local students had become involved in the project. The next stage is expected to expand the effort further. The Nation reported plans to install 10 large artificial nests in protected forest areas. Yanin has also been raising funds to support the installation of additional nests in ‘Su-ngai Padi National Park’ in Narathiwat province, which provides habitat for endangered hornbill species, including the Helmeted Hornbill and Rhinoceros Hornbill.Why does education remain an important part of Homes for HornbillsFor Yanin, conservation does not end once an artificial nest is placed in a tree. The initiative also works with children and young people to explain the role hornbills play in forest ecosystems. Hornbills help disperse seeds, making them important to forest regeneration and biodiversity. Yanin has also used storytelling to spread awareness. According to Khaosod English, she produced the documentary ‘Homes for Hornbills,’ which ranked among Thailand’s top 10 youth documentaries. Her project shows how a conservation idea can begin with a simple observation that ‘a bird needs a safe place to breed, while plastic waste needs a better destination than the rubbish bin.’ By connecting those two problems, the 17-year-old has created a solution that has already helped hornbills and brought international attention to the challenges they face. More importantly, Homes for Hornbills demonstrates that meaningful conservation work does not always have to begin with a large organisation or decades of experience. Sometimes, it can start with an idea to make something that can actually be used in the forest.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.summary: US News: The US Navy’s aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln arrived in Thailand on Wednesday after 286 days at sea. The authorities in nearby Pattaya stepped u.
articles.body: The US Navy’s aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln arrived in Thailand on Wednesday after 286 days at sea. The authorities in nearby Pattaya stepped up patrols and raided suspected prostitution venues amid arrival of thousands of American military personnel.Police detained around 40 to 50 people during raids over the weekend for suspected involvement in prostitution, news agency Reuters reported citing officials. Additional patrols have been deployed around Pattaya’s main beachfront and nightlife district during the carrier’s five-day port visit.The nuclear-powered Lincoln, carrying around 5,000 sailors and Marines, had been deployed since November 2025 and took part in the US naval blockade and combat operations during the war with Iran. Its deployment has lasted far longer than the Navy’s usual six- to nine-month cycle.Thai officials said the port visit is for rest, recuperation and logistics and is not connected to the Middle East conflict.Rear Admiral Robert E Loughran, commander of Carrier Strike Group 3, said, "What this strike group ​has accomplished is truly historic. I could not be prouder of the exceptional professionalism and expertise demonstrated ⁠by every member ‌of this team during our operations."The prolonged deployment comes amid reports of mental health concerns and deteriorating conditions aboard the carrier. The Lincoln and an accompanying guided-missile destroyer were seen with rust and mottled paint along their waterlines after the lengthy time at sea.The arrival is also expected to bring a business boost to Pattaya, a major tourist destination known for its nightlife. Around 40 buses will transport military personnel between the city and Laem Chabang.Pattaya Mayor Poramase Ngampiches said personnel would be prohibited from activities including water sports, jet skiing, bungee jumping, wrestling and boxing.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Congo's Ebola death toll crosses 3,000 amid worst outbreak in country's history; cases top 6,100
articles.summary: Rest of World News: More than 3,000 people have died in the Democratic Republic of Congo's Ebola outbreak, with confirmed cases crossing 6,100 as authorities struggle to .
articles.body: More than 3,000 people have died in the Democratic Republic of Congo's Ebola outbreak, with confirmed cases crossing 6,100 as authorities struggle to contain the country's worst-ever epidemic.Latest data from Congo's ministry of health showed that 6,186 confirmed cases and 3,007 deaths have been recorded since the outbreak was declared in Ituri province on May 15.According to Reuters, some health officials and experts believe the outbreak may have begun as early as January.The outbreak, caused by the rare Bundibugyo species of Ebola, has become the largest and deadliest in Congo's history after surpassing the 2018-2020 epidemic.It has spread to six provinces and remains the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak ever, according to news agency AP.Efforts to contain outbreak face major challengesHealth experts have cited weak surveillance systems, insecurity and community resistance among the factors hampering efforts to identify and treat patients early.The World Health Organisation estimates that around 60% of deaths occur outside treatment centres, according to Reuters, underlining the difficulty of detecting cases before patients succumb to the disease.Conflict in eastern Congo, where the outbreak is concentrated, attacks on health workers, inadequate health infrastructure and constant movement among miners have further complicated the response.The World Health Organisation has said the outbreak is on track to exceed the deadliest Ebola epidemic on record, the West African outbreak between 2014 and 2016, which infected more than 28,600 people and killed over 11,000 across Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone.Schools reopen amid transmission concernsThe start of a new academic year has also raised concerns about possible transmission in classrooms. Schools reopened across Congo on Tuesday despite calls from the teachers' union in Ituri, the epicentre of the outbreak, to delay the resumption of classes.Some government-owned schools in Ituri recorded low attendance, while a parent in Bunia said she was keeping her child at home.“I do not really see an increase in prevention measures,” said Aimerance Vahweka, a parent in Bunia, as cited by AP.Education officials said some schools were being equipped with noncontact infrared thermometers, hand sanitisers and hand-washing basins.“We also raise student awareness about adhering to hygiene protocols, particularly regular handwashing and the use of hand sanitiser,” said Etienne Ndjabu, a teacher at a private school in Bunia.However, many schools lack access to clean water and funding remains below target. “There are also significant logistical challenges, particularly in remote areas, where the delivery of equipment and learning materials may be delayed,” Greg Ramm, director for Save the Children in Congo, said.According to available health data, children aged four and below have the highest case-fatality rate of any age group in the outbreak, at 60%.No approved vaccine or treatment for BundibugyoThere is currently no approved vaccine or treatment specifically for the Bundibugyo species of Ebola that caused the outbreak.Several vaccines are under development, including candidates from the University of Oxford and the International AIDS Vaccine Initiative, according to Reuters.Congolese authorities have begun vaccinating frontline health workers with Merck's Ervebo vaccine, which is licensed against the Zaire species of Ebola and is believed to offer some cross-protection against Bundibugyo.Britain, meanwhile, announced more than £50 million ($67.56 million) in new funding on Tuesday to support efforts to contain the outbreak.The latest commitment brings Britain's total contribution to £78 million, with the funding aimed at supporting disease surveillance, frontline health workers, treatment access, infection control, community outreach and safe burials.“As the outbreak intensifies, we are accelerating our response to match the pace and scale of the challenge,” Britain's minister for Africa Kirsty McNeill said.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Buckinghamshire pub's manager stabbed to death in Germany
articles.summary: Rebecca Bullock, 31, was attacked at Rosenheim station on Sunday.
articles.body:
A pub has paid tribute to its "beloved" manager after she was stabbed to death in Germany.

Rebecca Bullock, 31, was attacked at Rosenheim station shortly before 01:00 local time (00:00 BST) on Sunday. She was taken to hospital but later died .

Bavarian Police said a 27-year-old German man, of no fixed address, was arrested at the scene and later detained in a psychiatric hospital on suspicion of murder.

The White Swan, in Whitchurch, Buckinghamshire, said: "We are so deeply sorry to say that our beloved Becca passed away over the weekend whilst away on holiday."

"Becca was much-loved by all of the team at the White Swan and our amazing locals," its Facebook post read.

The pub closed from Monday after what it described as a "tough few days", but its landlords said it would reopen from 15:00.

They said: "We know this is what Becca would have wanted."

A Foreign Office spokesperson told the BBC: "We are supporting the family of a British woman who died in Germany [and] are in touch with the local authorities."

The 31-year-old ran the London Marathon in 2022 in aid of the Milton Keynes-based Spinal Injuries Association, having recovered undergone three spinal operations.

She was also a member of Thame Runners in Oxfordshire, which said it was "deeply saddened" by her death.

In July, she and her clubmates were part of the winning women's team at the Waddesdon 5K in Buckinghamshire.

"She will be remembered with great affection by the many members who knew her, ran alongside her and shared in her love of running," the club said.

articles.title: 161-acre California racetrack closes after nearly 90 years of horse racing, now a $175 million plan could turn the site into a major waterfront park with $125 million in state funding
articles.summary: US News: Golden Gate Fields, a 161-acre racetrack in California that closed in 2024 after 83 years of horse racing, could get a new future as a major waterfron.
articles.body: Golden Gate Fields, a 161-acre racetrack in California that closed in 2024 after 83 years of horse racing, could get a new future as a major waterfront park near Berkeley. The state's lawmakers have proposed setting aside $125 million in state funds to support the plan.The funding would come from Proposition 4, a climate bond approved by California voters in 2024, San Fransisco Chronicle reported. The proposal was introduced by state Sen Jesse Arreguin and is aimed at helping transform the former racetrack into a regional public park along the East Bay shoreline.“This is a once-in-a-generation opportunity to reclaim 161 acres of East Bay waterfront for the public, and we are seizing it,” Arreguin said in a statement.The proposed park would open up a large stretch of waterfront that was previously occupied by the racetrack. Plans include better access for pedestrians and cyclists and a connection between existing parks and protected open spaces in the area. The property also has views of the Golden Gate Bridge, San Francisco, Mount Tamalpais and the Marin Headlands.The proposal comes after years of debate over what should happen to the Golden Gate Fields property. The racetrack was the Bay Area’s last remaining horse racing venue when it closed in 2024.Nonprofit plans to buy siteThe Trust for Public Land announced in March that it intended to purchase the property and preserve it as a park. The national nonprofit, which acquires land for parks and conservation, has been working with local officials, conservationists and community groups on the proposed acquisition.The organisation agreed to purchase the land if it could raise the required $175 million before the end of 2026. It had about $20 million available when it entered the purchase agreement, according to a report by Bay City News Service.The proposed $125 million state contribution would therefore provide most of the remaining funding needed to complete the purchase. However, the money is not yet guaranteed. The proposal remains subject to approval through the state budget process.Connecting open spacesThe proposed park would not stand alone. According to Arreguin’s office, the park could connect Albany Beach with McLaughlin Eastshore State Park. The proposal would also create a larger continuous open-space area linking Albany Beach, McLaughlin Eastshore State Park, Point Isabel Regional Shoreline, Albany Bulb and Brooks Island Regional Preserve.The Trust for Public Land plans to donate the property to the East Bay Regional Park District after purchasing it. The land is divided between the city boundaries of Albany and Berkeley. The proposed park would include a mix of recreational facilities and open space.“With this $125 million investment, Golden Gate Fields can go from a shuttered racetrack to one of the great waterfront parks in California,” Arreguin said. He added that the community had fought for the land to have a future where it could be open to everyone rather than remaining behind fences.From horse racing to public open spaceGolden Gate Fields opened in 1941 and became a major horse racing venue in the Bay Area. Racing was suspended during World War II before resuming in 1947. The venue eventually became the Bay Area’s last racetrack. Its closure in 2024 ended 83 years of horse racing at the site.Arreguin, who was Berkeley’s mayor when the closure was announced, supported turning the property into public open space. Earlier this month, environmentalists and community members testified before a state Senate budget subcommittee in support of funding for the park proposal. Berkeley civic leaders Loni Hancock and Tom Bates also spoke in favour of the plan, according to Arreguin.For now, the proposed transformation depends on the state budget process. If lawmakers approve the $125 million allocation, the funding could help the Trust for Public Land complete its planned purchase and move the former racetrack closer to becoming a public waterfront park.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: US couple kept 4 kids captive in truck for over 6 years, sexually abused them: Authorities
articles.summary: US News: Four children were allegedly kept captive inside the sleeper cab of a semi-truck for more than six years, denied schooling, adequate food and medical .
articles.body: Four children were allegedly kept captive inside the sleeper cab of a semi-truck for more than six years, denied schooling, adequate food and medical care, and sexually abused while the vehicle travelled between Atlanta and Miami, authorities said.According to the New York Post, Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier said Tuesday that the children — two boys and two girls — were sexually abused and mistreated while in the care of Keysha Monique Epps, 51, of Atlanta, and Tamra Marshon Stewart, 37, of Jacksonville.The children were allegedly confined to the truck and rarely allowed to leave.Authorities said the children, who were between five and nine years old when the alleged abuse began, shared a single bunk in the truck's sleeper cab. They were allegedly denied adequate food, hygiene, education, and medical and dental care.The two girls told investigators that Stewart sexually abused them for years, while the two boys allegedly witnessed the abuse and were physically assaulted after confronting Stewart or reporting it to Epps, authorities said.Uthmeier described the truck as a “rolling dungeon”, saying the adults would sometimes stop at truck stops to use the restroom or shower but leave the children locked inside the cab.Investigators said the children suffered severe health problems after years of alleged neglect. A detective reportedly noticed that they walked with an unnatural gait, which authorities attributed to prolonged confinement.One child told investigators that she suffered a severe burn from cooked noodles but was not taken for medical treatment, leaving her with a permanent scar.Another child was diagnosed with an untreated sexually transmitted infection after leaving the pair's custody, according to authorities.The alleged abuse and confinement continued from January 2020 through April 2026, authorities said. Investigators intervened after receiving a tip and subsequently removed the children from the truck.Stewart faces multiple charges, including sexual battery by a person in familial or custodial authority, lewd or lascivious molestation of a child under 12, battery of a child and child neglect causing permanent disfigurement.Epps faces multiple charges including sexual battery by a person in familial or custodial authority, lewd or lascivious molestation of a child under 12, child neglect and failure to report child abuse.“This case is one of, if not the most, horrific that my team has ever had to work on,” Uthmeier said, adding that the children were now safe but faced a “long road to recovery”.Authorities said the investigation remains ongoing and additional charges could be filed.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: China planted a huge forest belt to fight desertification; scientists say the trees are creating a carbon-versus-water trade-off
articles.summary: Rest of World News: In November 2024, China completed a 3,046-kilometre green belt around the Taklamakan Desert, filling the final gaps in a project that has been under c.
articles.body: In November 2024, China completed a 3,046-kilometre green belt around the Taklamakan Desert, filling the final gaps in a project that has been under construction for decades. The belt forms part of the Three-North Shelterbelt Program, launched in 1978 as one of the world's largest ecological restoration efforts, designed to combat desertification, reduce the movement of sand and protect land across northern China. Now, researchers are examining another consequence of that transformation: how the expanding vegetation is changing the relationship between carbon and water across the region. A 2026 study titled Nonlinear carbon–water coupling in terrestrial ecosystems: Insights from China’s Three-North Shelterbelt Forest region, published in Regional Sustainability, analysed changes in net primary productivity, carbon use efficiency and water use efficiency across the Three-North Shelterbelt region between 2000 and 2020. The researchers found that both productivity and water use efficiency increased significantly, while carbon use efficiency showed a small, statistically insignificant decline, revealing a much more complicated picture than simply measuring whether the landscape has become greener.How researchers tracked 20 years of carbon and water dynamics across the shelterbeltThe study examined the spatial and temporal behaviour of three measures used to understand how vegetation handles carbon and water: net primary productivity, carbon use efficiency and water use efficiency. Researchers analysed the Three-North Shelterbelt Forest region across different climatic zones and vegetation types, using satellite and environmental datasets together with machine-learning and statistical modelling techniques. Between 2000 and 2020, net primary productivity increased at an average rate of 2.69 grams of carbon per square metre per year, while water use efficiency increased by 0.004 grams of carbon per kilogram of water per year. Both trends were statistically significant. Carbon use efficiency, by contrast, declined by approximately 5.40 × 10⁻⁴ per year, but that change was not statistically significant. The researchers also found that the relationship between water use efficiency and productivity was substantially stronger than the relationship between carbon use efficiency and productivity. Leaf area index was identified as the most important influence on both NPP and WUE, while elevation had the strongest influence on CUE. Rather than finding one simple response across the entire shelterbelt, the study found that the relationships between vegetation, climate and carbon-water processes were nonlinear and varied according to environmental conditions.Why increasing water use efficiency does not necessarily mean the forests are using less waterThe distinction between productivity and efficiency is important because water use efficiency does not simply mean that vegetation is consuming less water. Instead, it describes the amount of carbon gained relative to the amount of water used. A rise in WUE can therefore occur when vegetation produces more carbon for a given amount of water, without necessarily proving that total water consumption has fallen. The 2026 study found that NPP and WUE rose together across the Three-North region, suggesting that vegetation became more productive and more efficient in its relationship with water over the period studied. At the same time, the researchers found that carbon use efficiency did not increase significantly, meaning that greater productivity did not translate into a statistically significant improvement in the fraction of carbon retained by the ecosystem. These findings do not establish that the shelterbelt is depleting groundwater, nor do they demonstrate a quantified carbon-versus-water trade-off. Instead, they show why the ecological effects of large-scale vegetation restoration cannot be judged from increasing greenery or carbon uptake alone. Water availability, climate, vegetation structure and geographic conditions all interact to determine how these ecosystems function.What satellite research found as the Taklamakan Desert became greenerA separate study titled Human-induced biospheric carbon sink: Impact from the Taklamakan Afforestation Project, published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences in January 2026 provides another piece of the picture by examining the Taklamakan Desert and surrounding areas over roughly two decades. Researchers analysed satellite measurements of vegetation cover and photosynthetic activity alongside atmospheric carbon dioxide and modelled carbon fluxes. They found a significant increase in vegetation cover and photosynthetic activity, with the strongest changes concentrated along the desert margins. Total green area increased by an estimated 162.2 square kilometres per year, while the researchers found that the greening areas had developed into stronger carbon sinks over the study period. The study linked the spatial pattern of this vegetation expansion to China's Three-North Shelterbelt project and concluded that the increased vegetation had enhanced the region's capacity to absorb carbon dioxide. The findings therefore reinforce one part of the newer research: China's long-running restoration efforts are not merely changing what the desert looks like from space, but are measurably altering its carbon cycle. At the same time, the two studies answer different questions. The Regional Sustainability paper examines the relationship between carbon and water indicators across the much larger Three-North Shelterbelt region, while the PNAS study focuses specifically on vegetation expansion and carbon uptake around the Taklamakan. Together, they show a landscape undergoing a profound ecological transformation, but they do not establish that China's green belt is simply “trading water for carbon.” The more defensible conclusion is that the restoration program is changing both carbon- and water-related ecosystem processes, and understanding whether those changes remain sustainable will depend on how vegetation responds to the region's highly variable climate and water availability in the decades ahead.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Quote of the day by Jim Carrey: "You can fail at what you don't want, so you might as well take a chance on doing what you love" — a powerful lesson on fear and failure
articles.summary: US News: Many people choose careers and life paths based on what appears safe rather than what they genuinely want. But Jim Carrey's famous observation challen.
articles.body: Many people choose careers and life paths based on what appears safe rather than what they genuinely want. But Jim Carrey's famous observation challenges the assumption that choosing the safer option protects us from failure."You can fail at what you don't want, so you might as well take a chance on doing what you love," Carrey said during a commencement speech in 2014. The message is simple but uncomfortable: failure is possible even when we make cautious choices. If risk cannot be completely avoided, fear alone may not be a good enough reason to abandon something that matters to us.Quote of the day by Jim Carrey "You can fail at what you don't want, so you might as well take a chance on doing what you love."Where this quote comes fromCarrey delivered the line while addressing graduates of Maharishi University of Management, now Maharishi International University, in 2014.The observation came from a deeply personal experience. Carrey told students that his father could have become a comedian but did not believe it was a realistic career. He instead became an accountant because it seemed like the safer choice.That security did not last. When Carrey was 12, his father lost his job and the family went through financial difficulties.Carrey said the experience taught him an important lesson: it was possible to fail at something you did not want to do in the first place. That realisation became the basis of one of the most remembered lines from his speech.What Jim Carrey's quote really meansThe quote is not a promise that following your passion will automatically lead to success.It argues something more practical. Choosing a conventional or apparently secure path does not guarantee that things will work out either.People often divide their choices into two categories: the risky thing they want to do and the safe thing they believe they should do. Carrey questions that distinction.Jobs disappear. Industries change. Businesses fail. Carefully planned careers can take unexpected turns. The supposedly safe choice therefore carries uncertainty too.If both paths contain risk, Carrey's argument is that fear should not automatically determine which one a person chooses.The safe option can fail tooPeople often associate failure with ambitious decisions such as starting a business, becoming an artist, changing careers or moving somewhere new.But staying where you are is also a choice.Someone can spend years pursuing a career they never particularly wanted and still lose the job. Another person might repeatedly postpone an ambition while waiting for ideal circumstances that never arrive.Carrey's quote changes the question from "What if I fail?" to something more revealing: "If failure is possible anyway, what is worth taking a chance on?"That does not eliminate the need for planning. It simply changes the role fear should play in making the decision.Fear can disguise itself as practicalityCarrey's wider commencement speech repeatedly dealt with fear and the choices people make because of it.There is an important difference between being practical and being afraid.Practicality means considering money, responsibilities, ability, timing and consequences before making a decision. Fear can sometimes make a person reject an opportunity before seriously testing whether it is possible.The two can easily look alike.Someone might say a career change is "unrealistic" when the deeper concern is the possibility of failure. Another person may keep postponing a creative ambition because there will always be a reason that makes waiting seem sensible.Carrey's message encourages people to recognise that difference.Failure does not always mean the choice was wrongFailure is usually treated as evidence that someone took the wrong path. But it can happen after sensible decisions as easily as after unconventional ones.A business might fail despite careful preparation. An actor might lose an audition despite doing everything well. Someone may apply for a dream job and be rejected.None of those outcomes automatically means the attempt was a mistake.Failure provides information. It may reveal what needs to change, what skills need improvement or whether another route would work better.Not trying produces a different problem: there may never be an answer.Why this idea remains relevant todayCareers today rarely follow one predictable route throughout a person's working life. People change industries, retrain, start businesses, build second careers and pursue opportunities that did not exist when they first entered the workforce.Technology and economic disruption have also weakened the assumption that a conventional career automatically guarantees long-term security.That does not mean everyone should quit a stable job and immediately pursue a dream.Taking a chance can also mean preparing carefully. Someone considering a different career can develop skills before leaving their current job. An aspiring entrepreneur can test an idea before investing heavily. A writer or musician can begin creating alongside other work.Risk does not have to mean recklessness.Other memorable quotes by Jim Carrey* "Fear is going to be a player in your life, but you get to decide how much."* "The effect you have on others is the most valuable currency there is."* "Your need for acceptance can make you invisible in this world."* "Risk being seen in all of your glory."These ideas reflect a recurring theme in Carrey's 2014 address: fear will always exist, but people still have some control over how much influence it has over their decisions.How to apply this quote in daily lifeStart by asking whether an important decision is being guided by genuine practical concerns or simply by fear of failure.If you want to change careers, identify the skills and financial preparation required. If you want to start something, test it on a smaller scale. If you want to write, perform, build or create, begin rather than waiting indefinitely for perfect circumstances.The lesson is not to ignore risk. It is to understand risk accurately.Then ask yourself: if the safer option can also fail, which possibility would you rather have genuinely tried?Why these words still inspire peopleCarrey's quote continues to resonate because it avoids one of the easiest promises associated with motivational advice. He does not say that doing what you love guarantees success.He says that avoiding what you love does not guarantee success either.His father's experience showed him that a seemingly secure choice could still end unexpectedly. The lesson Carrey drew from it was not that people should behave recklessly, but that fear should not be mistaken for certainty.Failure may exist on either road. Sometimes the more meaningful question is deciding which road is worth the attempt.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Iran attacks US sites after American strikes, wedding deaths
articles.summary: Iran launched a wave of attacks on US sites across the Middle East on Wednesday as violence surged after an extensive American bombardment and the deaths of...
articles.body:
Iran launched a wave of attacks on US sites across the Middle East on Wednesday as violence surged after an extensive American bombardment and the deaths of four people at an Iranian wedding party.

Iran's Revolutionary Guards announced attacks on US bases in Jordan, the UAE, Kuwait, Bahrain and Iraq's autonomous Kurdistan region, in the six-month conflict's heaviest exchange in weeks.

US President Donald Trump had warned earlier of "much harder and higher" attacks if Iran retaliated to the US strikes, which Iran's military and state media said killed 18 people.

The renewed attacks deepen the impasse in the war, as Iran maintains a stranglehold on the Strait of Hormuz oil export route while the US presses a counter-blockade of Iranian ports.

In the latest strikes, the Iranian Red Crescent said on Tuesday that four people including a child were killed and more than 50 people were wounded by a US attack at a wedding in Iran's south.

A video shared by an Iranian government account showed debris and damage at what it said was the wedding site in Sirik following a US strike, with people heard screaming in the background.

"Unfortunately, this is a residential building. And unfortunately, this happened during my daughter's wedding ceremony," Ali Mallahi, father of the bride and owner of the building, said in a video carried by state TV.

"It is a very saddening incident... Thank God the casualties were not higher."

Iran's top negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf lashed out over the wedding attack, calling the United States "Satan".

"If a power acts like Satan, picks targets like Satan, and kills like Satan, it's Satan," he posted on X.

The US military did not address the incident directly.

US Central Command (CENTCOM) spokesman Tim Hawkins said "the US military never targets civilians, unlike the IRGC", referring to Iran's Revolutionary Guards.

The latest round of fighting began when Washington hit Iranian targets on Sunday, the first known strikes in several weeks.

Tehran's forces then targeted US troops in Jordan and the United Arab Emirates, and projectiles struck two oil tankers in unclaimed attacks.

Two Filipino sailors died in one of the tanker attacks on Monday, Saudi Arabia's national shipping company said Wednesday.

Trump said the US strikes were "in retaliation for the Iranians' failed attempt at adding sea mines to the Strait" and firing missiles at the base in Jordan.

More US attacks came on Tuesday, with Iranian state TV reporting explosions in the south along Hormuz and on an island in the Gulf, and that US forces hit an airport in the southern province of Kerman.

Seven people were killed and eight others wounded in a missile attack in the southern Khuzestan province, IRNA reported.

The Guards said four personnel were killed in a US strike in the Kermanshah province, and three paramilitaries died in an attack on Lavan island in the Gulf.

It said Iran's retaliatory strikes included "a coordinated missile and drone attack on US bases in Erbil", according to a statement carried by the state-run IRNA news agency.

The Guards also announced a missile attack on a US Marine training camp in Jordan on the Gulf of Aqaba, near the Saudi and Israeli borders, according to Iran's Tasnim news agency.

In the Gulf, air raid sirens sounded in Bahrain and also Kuwait, where authorities said an Iranian drone set off a blaze at a residential complex.

Ghizlan Saad, a Bahraini mother of two, said the sirens woke her family in the middle of the night, "bringing back memories of the attacks, of the fear and apprehension".

"I hope the situation resolves quickly, especially since we have just started the new school year after a year overshadowed by wartime conditions," she added.

The war began in late February with US-Israeli attacks on Iran that killed its supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.

A fragile ceasefire collapsed after attacks on commercial ships in the Hormuz strait, through which one-fifth of world oil supplies previously flowed.

Incidents in the strait have continued. Iran's Guards said Wednesday that two oil tankers caught fire after hitting mines "at the urging of the US military to transit via an illegal route".

Trump warned on his Truth Social platform Tuesday that if Iran retaliated to US attacks, "they will be hit again at a much harder and higher level, but it will not be the biggest attack of them all".

"There will be very little left of the Islamic Republic of Iran!" he wrote.

Despite the soaring tensions, Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian vowed on Tuesday to match any US move to return to a deal aimed at ending the war.
authors: AFP bureaus in Tehran, Washington and Dubai

articles.title: Body of missing British trekker Alexander Harris found in northern Pakistan
articles.summary: The 30-year-old from Birmingham went missing on Saturday as he was descending from Musa Ka Musala.
articles.body:
The body of a British trekker has been found in northern Pakistan, local officials have said.

Alexander Harris, who was originally from Birmingham, went missing on Saturday as he was descending from the summit of Musa Ka Musala, a mountain of just over 4,000m (13,000ft), in the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province.

Khalid Iqbal, the area's deputy commissioner, said police and volunteers had been involved in a search for 30-year-old Harris and his body was found on a path in a forest, adding "most probably he slipped and fell".

He had been living in Pakistan's capital Islamabad where he worked for global advisory company Adam Smith International.

Harris, who also had Irish citizenship, had set off on the trek around 05:40 local time on Saturday with a hiking companion. They took some photos at the summit and then began to descend, before becoming separated.

"There was a difference in their speed," Iqbal said. "He [Harris] was moving faster, he got about 1-2km ahead. Then it started raining."

The deputy commissioner estimated that between 250-300 people were involved in the rescue operation including police and volunteers, searching on foot and with drones, although their use was limited by poor visibility.

A keen hiker and trail runner, Harris was a regular participant in long distance races in Pakistan.

Iqbal said the two trekkers had not told the authorities about the trip.

"The hotel had offered him a guide and police security," Iqbal says. "But he said that he knew the area and did not need any help."

In a statement, Adam Smith International said Harris was a "much loved member" of their team and that they were devastated by his death.

His company said: "He cared deeply for Pakistan, its people, its nature, and learned Urdu during his time there."

It added: "We are deeply grateful to the hundreds of people who joined the search effort, including local residents, volunteers, police, rescue teams, forest department, members of Alex's trail running community, and the government of Pakistan that supported the operation.

"They searched tirelessly in difficult conditions, often in heavy rain, fog and poor visibility, over steep and challenging terrain."

It said: "Our thoughts are with Alex's family, friends and colleagues at this incredibly difficult time. We remain focused on supporting his family."

Harris's running group, Margalla Trail Runners, posted on social media calling him "a passionate trail runner".

They added: "May his soul rest in peace and may his family and loved ones find strength and comfort during this difficult time."

The UK Foreign Office has been contacted for a response.

articles.title: Criminals publish data of 8.7m people after Manchester Airports Group hack
articles.summary: The company, which owns Manchester, Stansted and East Midlands airports, was hacked last month.
articles.body:
Criminal hackers have posted the personal data of nearly nine million people online after breaching three UK airports .

Hackers extorted Manchester Airports Group (MAG) for an undisclosed amount but failed to get their ransom paid.

Customers of Manchester, London Stansted and East Midlands airports are being warned of secondary attacks as the data is now available to other criminals.

"MAG is confident that we have taken effective measures to protect our customers and we have contacted all those affected, including reaching out to all those with upcoming bookings to advise them of additional support," the company said in a statement.

Contact details, vehicle registrations and postcodes were stolen in the breach that appears to have accessed databases containing wi-fi log in and car parking details.

The cyber-crime group - which the BBC is not naming - is offering the entire data set for free to other criminals or scammers through their website.

"Today we are releasing the Manchester Group database," they wrote.

"Half a terabyte, and every byte of it is pure PII [personally identifiable information]."

Stolen data experts at HaveIBeenPwned have analysed the published material and confirmed it contains people's email addresses, phone numbers, addresses, licence plate numbers, purchasing history and browsing device data.

Cyber-security expert Kevin Beaumont warned those affected to be on high alert for other forms of scam and hack - especially high profile or wealthy individuals.

"The data includes both historical locations and planned future travel, so individuals sensitive to their movements being known may need to take precautions," he said.

"People should be alert to scammers reusing the data and so knowing details such as phone numbers and car registration numbers," he added.

MAG says it is working with the authorities and specialist advisors and says passengers' physical safety has not be at risk in the airports.

Unusually, the cyber criminals' website where the MAG data is available is hosted on the clear internet and not on the dark net like most other so-called hacker "leak sites".

This makes the data easier to access, increasing the risk to victims of MAG and the other companies the gang has breached in recent months.

As well as posting the stolen data, the hackers boasted about how they breached each victim using the same method each time - exploiting weaknesses in how companies store their digital keys for internal networks.

Data watchdog the Information Commissioner's Office has advice on its website for people whose data has been hacked. It includes:

Report any details of stolen documents including passports, credit cards or driver's licences to the issuer

Check your bank statement and credit report for any unusual activity

Keep alert for any suspicious emails, messages or phone calls

Use strong passwords and multi-factor authentication for online accounts

Hackers steal data from millions of airport customers

UK cyber chiefs say it's time to ditch passwords for passkeys - what are they?

articles.title: King Charles, Macron and Burnham to get preview of Bayeux Tapestry at British Museum
articles.summary: British and French leaders will be at the British Museum to see the exhibition of the historic Bayeux Tapestry.
articles.body:
King Charles, French President Emmanuel Macron and UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham are to preview one of the blockbuster cultural events of the year, when they get to view the Bayeux Tapestry at the British Museum.

The visit on Wednesday comes ahead of the medieval tapestry going on public display in London from 10 September.

The 70m (230ft) tapestry, originally embroidered in England but kept for centuries in France, tells the story of the Norman Conquest and the Battle of Hastings in 1066.

President Macron said the loan of the national treasure until July 2027 was a "powerful symbol" of the close ties between the UK and France.

King Charles and Queen Camilla, Andy Burnham and his wife Marie-France van Heel, and Emmanuel Macron and Brigitte Macron will be shown key scenes in the tapestry, including the Coronation of King Harold and his death in battle.

School children from the UK and France will attend the event, with the King and the French president expected to make speeches marking the historic loan.

Sending the tapestry to the British Museum had been announced by Macron during the French state visit to the UK in July 2025, as an emblem of the strong partnership between the countries.

There had been some worries that moving the fragile tapestry could risk causing damage, but French government sources said ahead of the royal preview: "The display conditions at the British Museum are ideal."

The French authorities welcomed the way that visitors in London would see the tapestry laying flat, rather than upright, with this believed to be better for the conservation of the fibres, sewn more than 900 years ago.

It is believed that the final scenes of the tapestry have been lost or destroyed, as it has not always had such careful owners. In the 18th Century, during the French Revolution, it was rescued from being cut up to make covers for soldiers' carts.

At a state banquet hosted by King Charles in Windsor, Macron had said the missing end of the tapestry was a symbol that "in the great mural of Franco-British history, the end is yet to be written - it is up to us to do it".

This trip to the British Museum will be the first official joint engagement carried out together by King Charles and Andy Burnham since he became prime minister in July.

Burnham said the tapestry exhibition would be a chance to celebrate the "shared heritage" between the UK and France.

"The return of the Bayeux Tapestry to England is a landmark moment in the history of our two nations," he said.

French government sources said the occasion will also be an opportunity for President Macron to get to know Burnham - with Macron being the first overseas leader to come to the UK since he took office.

Support for Ukraine, the conflict in the Middle East, and relations with the European Union will be among the topics for the two leaders, say French sources.

Small boats crossing the Channel are likely to be discussed, as well as those Norman versions embroidered on the tapestry.

The Bayeux Tapestry records a much earlier chapter in Anglo-French relations, when King William of Normandy fought King Harold for the throne of England.

Using dyed wool stitched onto linen, it shows the competing claims to the throne, the Normans sailing across the Channel and the decisive Battle of Hastings, in which Harold was killed, allowing William the Conqueror to become monarch.

The tapestry, believed to have been embroidered by English women for the new Norman rulers in the 1070s, includes 58 separate scenes, with 627 human figures, 737 animals, 37 ships and 23 trees, with a Latin narration accompanying the images.

As part of this cultural diplomatic exchange, the UK is lending France one of the British Museum's prize exhibits - treasures from the Anglo-Saxon Sutton Hoo burial.

Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy said: "Britain and France have a unique shared history and nothing symbolises it more than the Bayeux Tapestry.

She said "a generation of British children will remember it for the rest of their lives".

There was strong demand for tickets to see the tapestry, with the exhibition already sold out until the end of 2026.

The next tickets, covering visits between January and March 2027, will be available from the British Museum from 21 October.
