articles.title: Family of murdered Stacy Hunter say new misogyny bill would not have protected her
articles.summary: First Minister John Swinney said he wanted to use his role to tackle violence against women.
articles.body:
The family of Stacy Hunter has called for immediate action to protect victims of domestic abuse, after plans for a misogyny bill were announced by the Scottish government.

First Minister John Swinney announced plans to recognise misogyny as a "distinct form of prejudice and abuse" during his programme for government on Tuesday, alongside a public health campaign to target toxic male behaviour.

Stacy was murdered by her estranged husband, Jim Mair, at her home near Houston in Refrewshire in July. He was on bail for attacking her. His body was found nearby.

Her family is calling for tougher action on offenders.

Speaking on BBC Radio Scotland's Mornings programme, Stacy's brother said some aspects of the proposals were important but they are not "anywhere near good enough".

We saw signs of domestic abuse, but we didn't know how to protect Stacy

Calls for GPS monitoring of domestic abuse suspects after murder

Woman found dead was murdered, police say, as man's death still 'unexplained'

Sean Hunter said he did not believe what happened to his sister was down to attitudes.

"If these bills and health campaigns were introduced 30 or 40 years ago and were successful, I don't think that would've stopped what happened," he said.

"People that are repeatedly offending and are dangerous, they are not listening to advice or taking on board what's right or wrong. They are choosing to do whatever they want to do.

"I think the main way of stopping that is more action towards reprimanding them, having real consequences to their actions and deterring them for doing that not trying to appeal to their better nature."

Swinney used his programme for government speech to say he would ensure "harassment and abuse based on misogyny is outlawed".

The bill is also expected to include proposals to recognise pregnancy as an aggravating factor in domestic abuse cases, and provide emergency funds for those leaving abusive partners.

Stacy's family said concerns for the "safety of people right now" have not been addressed.

Her relatives are backing a campaign calling for high-risk domestic abuse perpetrators or suspects released on bail to have their location monitored using GPS equipment.

This could include individually assessed exclusion zones around victim's homes or workplaces, and alerts that trigger police responses when conditions are breached.

Scottish ministers have previously faced criticism over the slow rollout of Global Positioning System (GPS) equipment, which is used far less in Scotland than in some other countries.

Justice Secretary Neil Gray said tackling violence against women and girls is a "top priority" for the government and part of that was addressing attitudes and influences.

Speaking on Mornings , he said: "We're taking steps at the moment to strengthen bail conditions and bail monitoring. We are looking to expand GPS technology, for instance."

Gray said the technology is available and he is looking to accelerate a "full roll-out and availability across the board" of the technology.

When asked if he could to commit to a roll-out by the end of the year, Gray said he "would check".

Stacy's mother Ann met the first minister last week to discuss the campaign. She said it "does seem like" Swinney wants to take action.

Sean Hunter said victims are consistently "let down" by their abusers being bailed. His sister's killer had been granted bail for attacking her three weeks before the murder.

The Hunters want more consideration for victims during the bail process, as well as more repercussions for breaking bail conditions.

Earlier, First Minister John Swinney said he had been "significantly affected" after meeting Stacy's mother - as well as domestic abuse survivor Danielle MacDonald - over the summer.

He told the BBC's Radio Scotland Breakfast programme: "I cannot begin to understand or appreciate the scale of suffering that all of the loved ones of the women who have lost their lives, or been affected by violence over the summer or all time, are experiencing.

"I want to use my role as first minister to do something about it."

Tackling violence against women has been a long-held mission for Scottish politicians.

But what will it take to truly root out what the first minister recently described as "an epidemic", and protect women who are at risk right now?

John Swinney spent much of the summer listening to survivors, families, and those working in the sector, as part of an effort to find the answers.

I'm told an early August meeting with Danielle MacDonald, who suffered at the hands of her husband for years, had a profound impact on him.

That, coupled with a series of tragic cases in recent weeks, spurred the government into action. It's clear Swinney is now personally invested in addressing the issue.

There's no doubt there will be cross-party backing for misogyny legislation, and a campaign to tackle behaviour has been well-received.

Likewise, organisations working in the sector have welcomed promises of multi-year funding and an end to a postcode lottery of provision - although they await the details.

Others are disappointed they did not hear more from the first minister on changes in the criminal justice system.

Of course, this is a complex, multi-faceted problem. And after making such a strong commitment on change, Swinney will be judged on whether he can deliver.

Radio Scotland Mornings have spoken to the Hunter Family as part of a series on violence against women - you can listen to the full programme here .

If you have been affected by any of the issues in this story, help and support is available at BBC Action Line .

articles.title: Former IDF soldier charged for affiliating himself with ISIS, watching terror training videos
articles.summary: The suspect, Khamis Su'ad, had served in the IDF between 2017 and 2019 and had allegedly exhibited a growing interest in ISIS since 2023. A former IDF soldie...
articles.body:
Former IDF soldier from northern Israel charged with training for terrorist purposes after allegedly preparing to join ISIS and fight in Syria or Africa.

Suspect watched ISIS killing videos, studied weapons use, and saved money for planned journey, according to the indictment.

Prosecutors argue that suspect poses a danger to public and state security, with no release conditions adequately addressing the risk.

The suspect, Khamis Su'ad, had served in the IDF between 2017 and 2019 and had allegedly exhibited a growing interest in ISIS since 2023.

A former IDF soldier from northern Israel was charged on Wednesday with training for terrorist purposes after prosecutors alleged that he prepared himself to join ISIS and fight for the organization in Syria or Africa.

Khamis Su'ad, 30, an Arab-Israeli resident of Huseiniya in the Galilee, was arrested on August 2 following a joint investigation by the Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) and Israel Police.

The prosecution filed the indictment in Haifa Magistrate's Court alongside a request to keep Su'ad in custody until the conclusion of the proceedings.

According to the indictment, Su'ad served in the IDF from 2017 to 2019. Beginning in 2023, he allegedly developed a growing interest in ISIS and came to identify with its activities, values, and objectives.

Prosecutors said he regularly visited websites and viewed social-media content associated with the terrorist organization.

In 2024, Su'ad allegedly decided to travel to Syria or Africa and fight for ISIS against those the organization considers infidels. According to the indictment, he then began preparing to carry out that plan.

Suspect allegedly watched ISIS killing videos, religious lessons

Prosecutors divided the alleged preparations into three areas. Su'ad watched videos showing killings and beheadings to prepare himself psychologically, studied weapons use and combat methods, and watched religious lessons delivered by senior ISIS figures. He also began saving money for the planned journey.

During 2026, he allegedly downloaded manuals and watched videos explaining how to produce missiles and drones, use sniper rifles and other weapons associated with ISIS, and employ military tactics.

Su'ad was charged with receiving training or instruction in operational methods and weapons for the purpose of advancing the activities of a terrorist organization or carrying out a terrorist act .

The charge does not require prosecutors to prove that he completed his alleged plan to travel abroad. They must, however, prove that the material amounted to training or instruction and that he received it for a terrorist purpose.

In the accompanying detention request, prosecutors said Su'ad admitted the conduct attributed to him during questioning. They also said investigators found videos and manuals on his phones that supported the allegations.

Prosecutors argued that Su'ad would pose a danger to the public and state security if released and that there was also a risk he could obstruct or evade the proceedings. They said no release conditions would adequately address that risk.

The detention request also states that Su'ad has no previous convictions.

Israel sees spate of ISIS-linked planned attacks

Su'ad's indictment follows at least two other ISIS-linked cases publicized by Israeli authorities in August.

On August 18, prosecutors charged Abdullah Gergawi, 20, from Segev Shalom , with allegedly planning to attack Beersheba's Forum nightclub using a vehicle rigged with explosives. Police said he had communicated with ISIS supporters and intended to join the organization in Syria.

On August 28, police and the Shin Bet announced that prosecutors would file indictments against a 16-year-old Galilee resident and Ibrahim Kaabiyya, a 19-year-old Haifa resident . Authorities alleged that the minor intended to attack Jewish police officers and soldiers on the Temple Mount, while Kaabiyya planned an attack against an IDF base in northern Israel. Kaabiyya's attorney denied that he had planned an attack and said his interest in ISIS material stemmed from curiosity.

Unlike those cases, the indictment against Su'ad does not identify a planned attack inside Israel. It rather concerns his alleged online training and preparations to travel abroad and fight for ISIS.

The court must now consider the prosecution's request to detain him through the trial. That decision is separate from the question of guilt and determines only where Su'ad will remain while the criminal proceedings continue.

articles.title: Russia strikes Ukraine injuring 8 as Moscow, Kyiv trade threats
articles.summary: Europe News: Russian airstrikes hit apartment buildings and civilian infrastructure in Ukraine’s Kyiv and Odesa regions overnight and into Wednesday morning, injur.
articles.body: Russian airstrikes hit apartment buildings and civilian infrastructure in Ukraine’s Kyiv and Odesa regions overnight and into Wednesday morning, injuring at least eight people including a child, local officials said.Ukraine’s Air Force said Kyiv and Odesa were among the regions worst hit in the latest wave of Russian attacks, the Associated Press reported.Russia launched 174 attack drones, including around half jet-powered drones, along with two ballistic missiles and two air-launched missiles, the Ukrainian Air Force said.The strikes caused significant damage in Odesa, where several floors of a 24-storey residential building were destroyed.Officials in the southern Odesa region said eight people, including a child, were injured in the attack. Several office buildings and two educational facilities were also damaged, while power outages disrupted electric public transport across the city.In the Kyiv region, a man and a woman suffered shrapnel injuries during morning attacks, regional military administration head Tymur Tkachenko said.Kyiv came under attack for the seventh consecutive day, although Wednesday’s strikes were less intense than those in previous days. A warehouse caught fire, while an educational facility and a medical practice were also damaged.The latest strikes came as the Russia-Ukraine war entered its fifth year, with fighting along the eastern and southern front lines largely stalemated and US-led efforts to broker a peace agreement yet to produce a breakthrough.Putin, Zelenskyy trade threatsRussian President Vladimir Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy exchanged threats late Tuesday, raising concerns over a possible escalation.Zelenskyy warned international airlines that Russian airspace could become increasingly unsafe as Ukraine expands its long-range drone campaign.“Russian airspace will effectively be closing,” he said, adding that the strikes were aimed at pressuring Moscow to accept peace negotiations.Putin accused Zelenskyy of engaging in “state terrorism” and said, “We don’t negotiate with terrorists.”Speaking at a news conference on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit in Kyrgyzstan, Putin also addressed reports that Ukrainian forces had used British-made drones to strike targets inside Russia.Asked whether Moscow could target British military facilities if the UK continues supplying weapons to Ukraine, Putin did not rule it out. With a slight smile, he said the answer was “a military secret,” the AP reported.China and North Korea have provided military support to Russia, while Iran has also backed Moscow in previous years.The exchange came as European officials considered measures in response to what they described as a broader Russian campaign of sabotage and disruption aimed at weakening support for Ukraine.Germany on Tuesday accused Russia of being behind an attempted attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport last month involving a drone reportedly carrying explosives.Russia reports Ukrainian drone attacksRussia’s defence ministry said its air defences shot down 130 Ukrainian drones overnight across 11 Russian regions, the annexed Crimean Peninsula and the Black Sea.In Russia’s Belgorod region, Ukrainian drone strikes killed two people and injured 16, acting Governor Alexander Shuvayev said. He added that the region had come under attack 140 times over a 24-hour period.Ukraine has increasingly used domestically produced long-range drones to target facilities inside Russia, including oil installations and warehouses operated by online retailers.Kyiv has said the attacks are intended to pressure Russia’s economy and make the impact of the war more visible to the Russian public.Russia’s push to capture more Ukrainian territory has lost momentum, according to Western officials and military analysts.The Institute for the Study of War said Russian territorial gains in August were only a fraction of those recorded during the same month last year.The Washington-based think tank said Russia’s spring and summer offensive had failed to break through Ukrainian defensive lines. “Russian gains remain slow and limited,” it added.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Reform up against 'complainants' society', Nigel Farage tells BBC
articles.summary: The Reform UK leader said a "whole ecosystem" didn't want "new kids on the block succeeding".
articles.body:
Nigel Farage has said the UK is a "complainants' society", as he faces ongoing questions about both his and his party's funding.

Speaking to the BBC ahead of the party's annual conference this week, the Reform UK leader said a "whole ecosystem" didn't want "new kids on the block succeeding".

It comes after a summer dominated by headlines about the party's finances and £5m he received from a party supporter before the last election.

Farage said he expects it "won't be too long" before he is interviewed as part of the ongoing parliamentary investigation into whether he should have publicly declared the sum upon his election as an MP.

The Reform UK leader said he hoped the investigation, which was launched in May but paused during the by-election he triggered in his Clacton seat, would "move a bit faster" now he had been re-elected to Parliament.

Farage has faced weeks of headlines about funding, including £5m he received before entering Parliament from Christopher Harborne, a Thailand-based British cryptocurrency investor and major Reform donor.

Parliament's standards commissioner is investigating whether he should have declared that sum upon becoming an MP in his published register of financial interests.

Farage has said the £5m was a personal gift and did not therefore require registration under the rules.

He continued to insist he believes he had done "nothing wrong", but ultimately it would be a "matter of interpretation" for the investigation to resolve.

Asked about the funding questions that have dogged the party over the summer recess, he said: "The point is, we live in a complainants' society.

"If you complain about me, automatically that triggers an investigation."

He said that political parties were "constantly writing to all the authorities", meaning Reform was "under investigation every day for virtually everything we do".

"There's a big picture here. The old two-party system that has dominated since the end of the First World War feels for the first time it faces an existential threat.

"There is a whole ecosystem with a century of development around this. And we come along from virtually nowhere and threaten the whole thing.

"So I think what you're seeing is the establishment, in a very co-ordinated way, fighting back."

Pressed on what he meant, he added: "I'm talking about normal human behaviour.

"People who hold positions of power, influence and money don't want new kids on the block succeeding. It's the whole ecosystem, it's everything."

articles.title: EU threatens Russia with new sanctions after Leipzig drone attack
articles.summary: European Union foreign ministers were consulting on Wednesday on how to respond to German allegations that Russia was behind a failed attack involving an exp...
articles.body:
EU foreign ministers are considering new sanctions against Russia in response to a failed drone attack at Leipzig airport, with possible measures including sanctions against 1,600 individuals and companies linked to Russia's military-industrial complex.

The EU has already implemented 21 sanctions packages on Russia since the start of its invasion of Ukraine in 2022, with the intention of weakening Russia's economic and military capabilities to continue the war.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen stated that Russia should expect more sanctions, emphasizing the need for the EU to respond faster and better to Russia's actions, including preparing sanctions to impose as soon as dangerous acts are attributed to Russia.

European Union foreign ministers were consulting on Wednesday on how to respond to German allegations that Russia was behind a failed attack involving an explosives-laden drone at Leipzig airport.

Possible measures include sanctions against a further 1,600 individuals and companies linked to Russia's military-industrial complex, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said on the sidelines of the ministers' meeting in Wicklow, Ireland.

More could potentially be added to the list, she said.

The EU has already agreed on 21 sanctions packages on Russia since the start of its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. The measures are intended to weaken Russia's economic and military ability to continue the war.

Kallas had announced work on new punitive measures last month, before Germany publicly blamed Russia on Tuesday for the drone discovered near Ukrainian cargo aircraft at the eastern German airport on August 4. The drone failed to detonate.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen also said that Russia should expect more sanctions.

"We're looking at ways to cut deeper into Russia's war chest," she said, speaking in Brussels alongside NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte.

Incidents like the one in Leipzig on August 4 mean that the EU has "to step up, and that means being ready to respond to Russia's recklessness faster and better."

This includes preparing sanctions and "have them ready to impose as soon as such dangerous, life-threatening acts are attributed. Every loophole Russia exploits is one we must close," von der Leyen said.

"Had this attack succeeded, this would have resulted in enormous damage and possibly even loss of life," she warned.

EU foreign ministers gathered in Ireland expressed their solidarity with Germany.

Kallas said that incidents like the one in Leipzig could serve as "wake-up calls" that "if we want to end this war, we all have to focus our efforts."

Ministers also discussed further support for Ukraine, including air defence, preparations for the coming winter and funding for additional assistance, as well as the possible use of frozen Russian assets.

The foreign ministers of Ukraine, Britain, Canada, Norway, Iceland, and Switzerland travelled to Ireland to attend the talks on aid for Ukraine.

In addition, EU ministers were expected to discuss developments in the Middle East.
